snippets.snippet_text: Jeremiah's priestly heritage connected him to the temple system he would later critique—a prophet called to confront the very institution of his lineage. This pattern mirrors how the Restoration emphasizes that truth-telling often requires standing against institutional corruption.

God doesn't comfort Jeremiah's self-doubt—he simply overrides it. 'Adequacy comes from the Sender, not from the capacities of the sent.' This principle mirrors modern covenant theology: when we enter temple covenants, we don't become adequate through our own merit but through divine partnership.

The Hebrew word 'yada' (to know) in God's commission of Jeremiah carries intimate relational knowledge—not distant observation. D&C 138 teaches that premortal spirits 'accepted their assignments' before mortality. Jeremiah was known and consecrated before his physical formation.

Israel abandons 'the fountain of living waters' (God) to dig 'broken cisterns that can hold no water'—a wordplay that captures spiritual bankruptcy in a single image. Jesus would later draw directly on this metaphor when offering the Samaritan woman 'living water.'

God opens the covenant lawsuit not with judgment but with remembrance: 'I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride.' Jeremiah's entire indictment rests on this—Israel has forgotten a love that God has not forgotten. The tragedy is not God's fickleness but Israel's amnesia.

Pagan nations maintain loyalty to their false gods, yet Israel—married to the living God—exchanges him for idols. The devastating irony: people bound by covenant to nothing prove more faithful than those bound by covenant to everything. This exposes that Israel's problem isn't ignorance but willful unfaithfulness.
